summary.text: The Cold War was a rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, lasting from after World War II until the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
It is called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly, though each backed opposing sides in regional proxy wars.
The rivalry showed up in an arms race, the Space Race, espionage, propaganda campaigns, embargoes and even sports diplomacy.

items.prompt: Why do historians call the US-Soviet rivalry a "cold" war?

options.label: It was fought mostly in freezing polar regions
The two superpowers never fought each other directly
Neither side ever built or tested nuclear weapons
It faded away quickly and left little lasting effect

items.explain: The word fits because the two superpowers did not fight directly, even though each backed opposing sides in regional conflicts.

items.prompt: A big power sends money and weapons to one side of a faraway country's conflict, while its rival backs the other side, and the two never fight each other. What was this called in the Cold War?

options.label: A proxy war, fought through other parties
A containment, meant to hold the rival in
An embargo, a ban on trading with the rival
A satellite state run directly by the rival

items.explain: Regional conflicts in which each superpower supported opposing sides are known as proxy wars.

items.prompt: After 1945, the USSR set up governments loyal to it across the Eastern Europe it occupied. What was the result for Europe?

options.label: The continent united under one shared alliance
Western Europe lost all contact with the US
Europe was politically divided by an "Iron Curtain"
Germany was quickly reunited under Soviet rule

items.explain: By 1949 the Soviet-installed governments helped split Europe, and Germany with it, along what was called the Iron Curtain.

items.prompt: The US wanted to stop communism from spreading and also help Western Europe's economies recover. Which pair of steps did that?

options.label: The Warsaw Pact and the Berlin Blockade
The Sino-Soviet split and the Korean War
The Hungarian Revolution and the Space Race
The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan

items.explain: The Truman Doctrine set out containment of communism in 1947, and the Marshall Plan in 1948 aided Western Europe's economic recovery.

items.prompt: In 1972 the US and USSR began signing treaties limiting their nuclear arsenals. What is that period called?

options.label: The Iron Curtain
Détente
The Sino-Soviet split
The Truman Doctrine

items.explain: Treaties limiting both sides' nuclear arsenals were signed during the period known as détente.

items.prompt: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and expanded political freedoms. What did that help bring about?

options.label: A new round of Soviet invasions in Eastern Europe
The Cuban Revolution and its communist government
The revolutions of 1989 and the Soviet collapse
A lasting alliance between the USSR and the US

items.explain: Gorbachev's wider freedoms contributed to the 1989 revolutions in the Eastern Bloc and to the collapse of the USSR in 1991.

paragraphs.heading: A war without direct fighting
paragraphs.text: The Cold War was a long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies: the capitalist Western Bloc against the communist Eastern Bloc. It began after the Second World War and ended when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. It is called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead, each backed opposite sides in regional conflicts called proxy wars.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Orwell wrote in The Observer in March 1946 that Russia had started a cold war against Britain and its empire. The first use of the term for the US–Soviet standoff came in an April 1947 speech by Bernard Baruch, an adviser to Democratic presidents, written by the journalist Herbert Bayard Swope. The columnist Walter Lippmann spread the term with his book The Cold War. Asked where it came from, Lippmann traced it to a French phrase of the 1930s, la guerre froide.

paragraphs.heading: Flashpoints
paragraphs.text: Early clashes included the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953 and ending in a stalemate. In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis began after the US placed missiles in Europe and the Soviets placed missiles in Cuba. It is widely seen as the moment the Cold War came nearest to nuclear war. The Vietnam War, from 1955 to 1975, was another major proxy war and ended in victory for North Vietnam. In Europe the Soviets tightened their grip by crushing the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 and through the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

paragraphs.heading: A struggle across the globe
paragraphs.text: As nearly all the colonies gained independence, many of them became Third World battlefields of the Cold War. Both powers offered economic aid to try to win the loyalty of countries that had not taken a side. The US supported anti-communist and right-wing dictatorships and uprisings. The Soviets funded left-wing parties, wars of independence and dictatorships.

paragraphs.heading: Thaw, chill and collapse
paragraphs.text: The Soviet Union and China fell out too: relations between them had broken down by 1961, and a border conflict in 1969 brought them to the edge of war. In 1972 the US opened contacts with China, and the US and the Soviet Union signed treaties limiting their nuclear weapons during a period known as détente. Tensions rose again in 1979, when governments allied to the US fell in Iran and Nicaragua and the Soviet–Afghan War broke out. Mikhail Gorbachev took over the Soviet Union in 1985 and widened political freedoms, which helped bring about the Eastern Bloc revolutions of 1989 and the Soviet collapse of 1991 that ended the Cold War.
